speechtext: The amendment now before the committee is a relatively minor one and at the time it was introduced I said that I did not think we would take specific exception to it. I see no reason why it should not be passed. I could then put before the committee an amendment which really embodies that to which we are taking the strongest exception. Will the chairman please read the amendment?

subtopic: BILL IN TERMS GENERALLY OF RELIEF ACT, 1933, WITH PROVISION RESPECTING DELAYED RELIEF ACCOUNTS
speechtext: The amendment is that section 2 (a) be amended by adding after the word "province" in the fourth line thereof the following words, "and to Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers Limited."

speakerposition: stagedirection

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: BILL IN TERMS GENERALLY OF RELIEF ACT, 1933, WITH PROVISION RESPECTING DELAYED RELIEF ACCOUNTS
speechtext:
I should like to move the following amendment:
That the section be amended by striking out the words "to take all such measures as in his discretion may be deemed necessary or advisable to maintain, within the competence of parliament, peace, order and good government throughout Canada."
This is an amendment to subsection (b) of section 2 and is seconded by Mr. Stewart (Edmonton). I would point out that the original section contains the words "notwithstanding the provisions of any statute or law the governor in council may" do the things which are mentioned in the amendment. I am proposing by the amendment that this power should not be given to the governor in council particularly as other powers to be given the governor in council which will remain in the section are ample to cope with every conceivable situation.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: BILL IN TERMS GENERALLY OF RELIEF ACT, 1933, WITH PROVISION RESPECTING DELAYED RELIEF ACCOUNTS
speechtext: How will the section read then?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: BILL IN TERMS GENERALLY OF RELIEF ACT, 1933, WITH PROVISION RESPECTING DELAYED RELIEF ACCOUNTS
speechtext:
If the amendment is agreed to the section will read as follows:
Notwithstanding the provisions of any statute or law the governor in council may,-
(a)	Upon such terms and conditions as may be agreed upon,-enter into agreements with any of the provinces respecting relief measures therein; grant financial assistance to any province and to Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers Limited by way of loan, advance, guarantee or otherwise; and in respect of such loans, advances and guarantees, may accept such security, enter into such agreements and generally do all such acts and things as the governor in council may deem necessary and expedient in the public interest;
(b)	When parliament is not in session to take all such measures as in his discretion may be deemed necessary or advisable to protect and maintain the credit and financial position of the dominion or any province thereof.
I feel certain the section, if left in that form, will be more than ample to meet any emergent condition which the Prime Minister or the government may ever be called upon to meet. I think these powers go much too far.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: BILL IN TERMS GENERALLY OF RELIEF ACT, 1933, WITH PROVISION RESPECTING DELAYED RELIEF ACCOUNTS
speechtext:
We cannot accept that amendment. It may be possible to meet one of the difficulties pointed out yesterday as to the meaning to be attached to the words
Relief Act, 1934

"notwithstanding the provisions of any statute or law." I have spoken to my colleague, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie), as to whether instead of the word "notwithstanding" we could insert the words "in addition to the powers conferred by any statute or law" dealing with matters affecting peace, order and good government in the country. There is some force to be attached to the criticism urged yesterday as to the meaning which might be put upon the word "notwithstanding." I do not think there would be a great difference as a matter of law but as that point was urged so strongly yesterday and if it clarifies in any sense the meaning of the section, we would be glad to change it. The amendment now proposed which provides for the elimination of any provision on the part of the executive to deal with matters affecting peace, order and good government, we cannot accept, for the reasons given yesterday. I thought at first that the amendment meant that these words would be retained but that the meaning would be modified in connection with the word "notwithstanding" but the right hon. gentleman proposes to eliminate these words entirely and we cannot accept his amendment.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: BILL IN TERMS GENERALLY OF RELIEF ACT, 1933, WITH PROVISION RESPECTING DELAYED RELIEF ACCOUNTS
speechtext: I had hoped that the amendment would carry but if the Prime Minister takes the view he does, I assume it will not. I trust the Prime Minister will nevertheless make the modification which he has suggested and alter the words "notwithstanding the provisions of any statute or law" to read "in addition to the provisions of any statute or law." It would make only a slight difference; the clause would still be objectionable, but what is proposed would be a modification.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: BILL IN TERMS GENERALLY OF RELIEF ACT, 1933, WITH PROVISION RESPECTING DELAYED RELIEF ACCOUNTS
speechtext:
We will prepare an
amendment along those lines. As the right hon. gentleman will observe, it will be necessary to retain these words in the first part of the section as there are statutes which do operate with respect to matters not concerned with peace, order and good government. These statutes refer to matters mentioned in that part of the section and the power to make agreements with the provinces to deal with those matters must be "notwithstanding the provisions of any statute or law." If the committee will permit this section to stand, the Minister of Justice and I will prepare an amendment which will eliminate the word "notwithstanding" in connection with peace, order and good government. If a meaning was to be given to this word, which I do not

attach to it, it would mean the conferring of power far beyond that which is intended. It is intended that the power to be conferred shall be conferred under the construction given by the privy council to the words "peace, order and good government." For the benefit of the committee I may say that that power by the executive is somewhat restricted when parliament is not in session. But if you interpret the words, as the right hon. gentleman did yesterday, in the light of "notwithstanding", it would be open to the construction of conferring upon the executive powers entirely beyond any statutes that now exist, and notwithstanding them. We will remedy that, and the Minister of Justice will prepare an amendment to meet it. But the first part of it, namely, the power of making arrangements with the provinces, and matters of that kind, must be notwithstanding any other provision that may exist elsewhere; these specifically named provisions must be the overriding provisions in connection with the arrangements made between the dominion and the provinces, and the amendment which we will prepare will, I think, meet the difficulty to which attention has been directed.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: BILL IN TERMS GENERALLY OF RELIEF ACT, 1933, WITH PROVISION RESPECTING DELAYED RELIEF ACCOUNTS
speechtext: That amendment may help to meet the one particular point mentioned, but there will remain the all-important question whether the power to pass orders in council with respect to peace, order and good government when parliament is not in session, in addition to any existing statute or law, should remain. I would suggest therefore that we continue the discussion on the main question rather than allow the section to stand. If, when it is disposed of, the other amendment is not ready, the section could then stand.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: BILL IN TERMS GENERALLY OF RELIEF ACT, 1933, WITH PROVISION RESPECTING DELAYED RELIEF ACCOUNTS
speechtext: That is quite satisfactory.

To touch upon another matter I would point out that the Minister of Labour yesterday cited from an order in council, the whole of which, he said, I had not given. He said he thought that I had omitted-quite unintentionally, he added-indicating that there had been audits prior to the passing of the item I was quoting from, namely, the order of March 12 of this year, being P.C. 222. "And whereas the audits and investigations which have been made and reported upon by the auditor general, in pursuance of the directions hereinbefore recited, have disclosed the necessity for a more extended audit of the accounts relating to relief expenditures if the interests of the dominion treasury are to be adequately safeguarded; . . . subtopic: BILL IN TERMS GENERALLY OF RELIEF ACT, 1933, WITH PROVISION RESPECTING DELAYED RELIEF ACCOUNTS
speechtext:
What is the amount of the lien notes outstanding in Saskatchewan for direct relief, and what justification is there for holding these notes, when direct relief was administered in other provinces without the taking of notes?
.Mr. GORDON:	Any notes taken in Saskatchewan were taken by the provincial government. I do not know the amount of the notes, but I have taken up with the provincial government the question of any adjustment that will be made if these notes are paid. The hon. member is however quite right; so far as I am aware, notes were not taken in the other provinces in the way in which they were taken in Saskatchewan. I am advised that in many instances, particularly in the southern part of the province, or the so-called drought area, where people were not bankrupt in the sense that they had no liquid assets, but had merely fallen upon misadventure by reason of crop failures, they requested that the relief granted be treated as an advance and tendered their notes for the assistance given. I have not the total amount of these notes, but the province will make an adjustment with the dominion government as and when any of them are paid.

subtopic: BILL IN TERMS GENERALLY OF RELIEF ACT, 1933, WITH PROVISION RESPECTING DELAYED RELIEF ACCOUNTS
speechtext:
A part of these notes
will be payable to the dominion government. Is it the intention of the dominion to accept that money or to refund it to the people who have executed the notes?

subtopic: BILL IN TERMS GENERALLY OF RELIEF ACT, 1933, WITH PROVISION RESPECTING DELAYED RELIEF ACCOUNTS
speechtext:
If any of the notes are
paid the total sum will be paid to the province of Saskatchewan and then an adjustment will be made as to any dominion portion of the notes, and that money will be refunded and will go into the consolidated revenue fund.

subtopic: BILL IN TERMS GENERALLY OF RELIEF ACT, 1933, WITH PROVISION RESPECTING DELAYED RELIEF ACCOUNTS
speechtext:
Do I understand the
minister to say that it will be refunded?

subtopic: BILL IN TERMS GENERALLY OF RELIEF ACT, 1933, WITH PROVISION RESPECTING DELAYED RELIEF ACCOUNTS
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: BILL IN TERMS GENERALLY OF RELIEF ACT, 1933, WITH PROVISION RESPECTING DELAYED RELIEF ACCOUNTS
speechtext:
To the persons who
pay the money?

Relief Act, 1934

subtopic: BILL IN TERMS GENERALLY OF RELIEF ACT, 1933, WITH PROVISION RESPECTING DELAYED RELIEF ACCOUNTS
speechtext:
Oh no; I am afraid I
have not made myself clear. The money, if paid at all, will be paid by the person who was assisted through the agency of the dominion government and the government of the province of Saskatchewan. If and when any of these moneys are repaid then an adjustment will be made between the two governments and any other contributors concerned, such as the municipalities.

subtopic: BILL IN TERMS GENERALLY OF RELIEF ACT, 1933, WITH PROVISION RESPECTING DELAYED RELIEF ACCOUNTS
speechtext:
That does not answer
the question. The position is this. The dominion has contributed a share of the moneys that went for direct relief in various provinces. In Saskatchewan the recipients of that direct relief in the rural areas were required to give notes. These notes were given to secure not only moneys advanced by the province but also moneys advanced by the dominion. When the recipient pays the note, the dominion government is entitled to an adjustment from the province and will get a part of the money. What justification can there be for the dominion holding thait money from the individual in Saskatchewan, while the government receives nothing from the individual in any other province?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: BILL IN TERMS GENERALLY OF RELIEF ACT, 1933, WITH PROVISION RESPECTING DELAYED RELIEF ACCOUNTS
speechtext: I think the hon. gentleman is confusing two things as he did the other evening in connection with wheat and never withdrew his statement. The truth is that when the dominion paid the whole amount as it did in 1930 and 1931 in the territory that was completely devastated, the people living there, having property that had once been very valuable, suggested that they give notes. Why I do not know, but they did. That information was communicated to us and they did give notes. Latterly they have not been giving notes for direct relief. The extent of my knowledge-this is before the present minister took office-is that it was only in the territory in which the crop was completely destroyed that they gave notes. If they make payments of the notes, .the money will be dealt with as may be thought desirable, but I do not think the hon. gentleman can make very much political capital out of it yet.

subtopic: BILL IN TERMS GENERALLY OF RELIEF ACT, 1933, WITH PROVISION RESPECTING DELAYED RELIEF ACCOUNTS
speechtext:
I am not trying to
nake political capital out of it; I will satisfy die Prime Minister on that score, but I find in the auditor general's report that relief granted in Saskatchawan and secured by lien notes of relief applicants amounts to $216,065.78.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: BILL IN TERMS GENERALLY OF RELIEF ACT, 1933, WITH PROVISION RESPECTING DELAYED RELIEF ACCOUNTS
speechtext: What year was that?

subtopic: BILL IN TERMS GENERALLY OF RELIEF ACT, 1933, WITH PROVISION RESPECTING DELAYED RELIEF ACCOUNTS
speechtext:
The period covered by the test audit was from October 10, 1930, to April 30, 1932. I do not know whether any lien notes have been taken since then and apparently the minister does not know. I asked him in the first place what the total amount of outstanding notes was and he says he does not know. Under that same item in the auditor general's report there is this:
Recoveries. Cash received from cash sales and from repayments by relief applicants, $8,129.59.
Apparently some of those relief applicants have paid back the money they received by way of direct relief. What I want to know is why direct relief recipients in Saskatchewan in a devastated area such as we have there should be called upon to repay this direct relief assistance that they got, whereas relief recipients in any other part of Canada were not required to do so.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: BILL IN TERMS GENERALLY OF RELIEF ACT, 1933, WITH PROVISION RESPECTING DELAYED RELIEF ACCOUNTS
speechtext:
The answer, as I said
to the hon. gentleman, is very simple. The dominion was paying the whole amount in the devastated area; there was no contribution by municipalities nor by the province and the entire obligation having been assumed by the dominion, it was indicated that some of the people desired to give notes. The number is apparently not very large because according to the report which the hon. gentleman has just read the sum between September, 1930, and the spring of 1932 was about $216,000. I thought the amount was larger. The sum of $8,000 has been repaid. To answer the question categorically, the only reason that notes were taken was that a desire was expressed to give them in that devastated area where the people still had their land that at one time had been worth a great deal of money. There was a feeling among many of them that they did not desire to regard themselves as being persons receiving relief or dharity, but rather getting a loan which they wished to pay back. The fact that some $8,000 have been repaid indicates that some persons desire to keep the faith they had in themselves by making this return of the money. In the other provinces in the other cases there was a threefold contribution by the municipalities, the province and the dominion. The dominion did not take notes nor was it suggested that it should. The dominion had nothing to do with the administration of the relief. The only place in which the dominion government has administered relief in this country since the depression came was in the devastated areas of Saskatchewan and for the reasons I have

Reliej Act, 1984
indicated a number of the people there gave notes at their own request and some have paid them off. In the other parts of the country the contribution was made by the dominion government to assist the provinces in the discharge of their duty and in every province at least in the west where they supplied seed grain, it will perhaps be recalled by the hon. gentleman that the statutes were amended to secure a lien with respect to seed that was supplied.

subtopic: BILL IN TERMS GENERALLY OF RELIEF ACT, 1933, WITH PROVISION RESPECTING DELAYED RELIEF ACCOUNTS
speechtext: Just one more question. I am not speaking on behalf of any of those who received relief by way of seed grain; I am inquiring in connection with those who received this direct relief for food, clothing and shelter. I gather from the Prime Minister's remarks that this sum of around $216,000 would represent money that was advanced in toto by the federal government and not contributed to in any way by the province. Apparently if these notes are collected, whether by the province or not, the money will belong to the dominion. I have still to receive an answer as to what will be done with it. While some may have requested that they should have the opportunity of giving notes there were numbers who were not too anxious to do so.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: BILL IN TERMS GENERALLY OF RELIEF ACT, 1933, WITH PROVISION RESPECTING DELAYED RELIEF ACCOUNTS
speechtext: They have not paid.

subtopic: BILL IN TERMS GENERALLY OF RELIEF ACT, 1933, WITH PROVISION RESPECTING DELAYED RELIEF ACCOUNTS
speechtext:
The notes are still outstanding against them as a liability and they see no way of paying them.
While dealing with this particular section in regard to entering into agreements with the provinces respecting relief measures, may I say that we have had in Canada great difficulty in finding markets for our wheat. In . that same area of Saskatchewan, I may call it the drought area, the farmers are finding great difficulty in getting seed and particularly feed for this year's operations. A few lines from a letter indicates just about what the situation is. This gentleman says:
This season we have the additional labour of this grasshopper campaign so that the commission's allowance is about one-third of enough.
That is the commission's allowance for feed. Then he says:
I threshed less wheat than I seeded last year.
Then he makes this suggestion:
In our district there is enough low grade wheat of last year's crop in elevators to relieve the feed situation and the danger of it again finding its way into market could be overcome by grinding before delivery to farmers.
In other parts of his letter he suggests that the farmers in the district in which he lives 74726-126J
will be happy to sign notes again if they can get feed to carry on their operations again this spring. He makes the suggestion that this low grade wheat of which the elevators there are full, might be used for the purpose of providing the required feed. I want to draw this matter to the minister's attention when we are considering granting relief to Saskatchewan.

subtopic: BILL IN TERMS GENERALLY OF RELIEF ACT, 1933, WITH PROVISION RESPECTING DELAYED RELIEF ACCOUNTS
speechtext: I would like to direct a question to either the Prime Minister or the Minister of Labour. During the time from 1930 to 1932, that the federal government was giving the entire relief, did all those who received relief give expression to the idea that they would like to pay it back and, if not, what percentage expressed the wish to pay it back?

subtopic: BILL IN TERMS GENERALLY OF RELIEF ACT, 1933, WITH PROVISION RESPECTING DELAYED RELIEF ACCOUNTS
speechtext: The department has not the records which would disclose the information asked for by the hon. gentleman. I do not know whether everyone expressed a desire to pay back the money granted to assist the people. I would be surprised if they did. But I would be pleased if the major portion of them did. The notes were taken by the province, as has been explained, and if the money is repaid there will be a refund to the dominion.

subtopic: BILL IN TERMS GENERALLY OF RELIEF ACT, 1933, WITH PROVISION RESPECTING DELAYED RELIEF ACCOUNTS
speechtext: From what source did the government get the information that the individuals receiving relief desired to pay it back? If the federal government, as stated by the Prime Minister, was paying 100 per cent, surely by reason of that fact the federal government would be in touch with the situation. Therefore I ask where they got the information that the individuals receiving the relief were desirous of paying it back. '

subtopic: BILL IN TERMS GENERALLY OF RELIEF ACT, 1933, WITH PROVISION RESPECTING DELAYED RELIEF ACCOUNTS
speechtext:
My recollection is that I

speechtext: A question of opinion is always a matter that is in no sense settled by the expression of one's views as against the views of somebody else. It need hardly be said to anyone who is familiar with the working of our constitution and the decisions under it that if the executive of the province is capable of exercising all the powers that the legislature can exercise under section 92 of the British North America Act, and can issue ordinances which have the effect of law, then the desirability of the dominion being in a position to take steps that may protect the federal interests goes without saying, and to legislate for peace, order and good government might conceivably be the only way in which it could be done. That is my view. That is the position which I present to the house as one of the not unimportant reasons why this legislation is sought. I merely mention it in passing as indicating a condition that was entirely different from the condition that prevailed a year ago. That provincial legislation, if in excess of provincial powers, may affect federal laws goes without saying because the books are full of cases in which that has happened. It happened in connection with a statute passed by the legislature of British Columbia regarding the sale of milk, and it was held by the privy council that the statute passed by the legislature was invalid because it encroached upon the federal power and was ultra vires of the provincial legislature. That was a statute that was published and was known to the federal authorities as a statute. If the province in the exercise of the power conferred upon the executive promulgates ordinances, this well may be the only way in which the federal power can be exercised because the ordinances, not being statutes, cannot be disallowed, and the only appropriate action would be under peace, order and good government.

speechtext: That is the point I was endeavouring to make. Assume they pass an ordinance of the type or character of the Milk Act which was declared to be ultra vires; we would have no way of dealing with that under the constitution except under peace, order and good government, because it it not a statute; it is an ordinance which is not subject to disallowance like a statute is subject to disallowance within a certain period of time, after having been certified by the Secretary of State and gone forward to the Minister of Justice who makes a report upon it, and the statute is then disallowed or left to its operation, as we say. But having no power to disallow an ordinance, if there is not a clear understanding by the province of the limitations imposed by the constitution upon the exercise of the power, the executive might enact ordinances that not only were not within section 92 of the British North America Act, but which contravened section 91. I am putting a case in which to await the decision of the courts might bring about a very grave disaster. It is a lawyer's point and one which unfortunately I cannot perhaps make very clear to my colleagues who are not of the legal profession. I am only pointing out a contingency which might arise, and which we are endeavouring to meet before it happens.

The British North

Undoubtedly it would be logical to disallow a statute of that kind but ever since the days of Mr. Blake, parliament has declared time after time that the question of the validity or invalidity of a provincial statute should be left to the operation of the courts. I think that has been the rule with but two exceptions. One was the instance dealt with by my right hon. friend in connection with the gypsum lands in Cape Breton, in which case the provincial statute was disallowed, I think under the advice of Mr. Lapointe, as.Minister of Justice. The other was in connection with a provision of the Companies Act, in which I think the advice was tendered by Sir Allen Aylesworth. The matter will have to be considered in due course when the statute is received, but it need not be received for a year. It has to be transmitted and that is an act over which we have no control.
An illustration used quite often is in connection with the Florence Mining Company. This was an Ontario statute and Sir Allen Aylesworth left it to its own operation and did not disallow. In that case a mining claim claimed by one man was declared by statute to be the property of another and it was provided that the one man should have no recourse to the courts. The case went to the privy council and although the committee may not be at all interested I might state that Sir Robert Finlay told me that he was doubtful as to the soundness of the decision. The decision was that the statute was within the legislative competence of the legislature, and its validity was upheld. The result was that by an act of the legislature of Ontario a mining claim was taken from one person and declared to be the property of another and as a result of that legislation he was declared to be unable to go into the courts for the
purpose of asserting his claim. That legislation was held to be valid and the then Minister of Justice, Sir Allen Aylesworth, did not disallow it. He left it to the operation of the law although my memory is that he made a report which indicated that he thought it was very unsound. But he did not substitute his views for those of the legislature which had validly exercised its powers.
I could give the committee other instances but I hope I have indicated to hon. gentlemen some of the thoughts which are in our minds with relation to a matter of such serious moment as that to which I have directed attention.

I should like to point out the force of that remark as it indicates where we can get to in matters of government once executives begin to take autocratic powers to themselves. The federal government at Ottawa has had this power to legislate with respect to peace, order and good government when parliament is not in session, and apparently that power has alarmed the provincial government. The provincial government has said: If we are going to have to bargain, we must have equally strong autocratic powers and be free to do what we wish. Notwithstanding all the laws and statutes, they took to themselves the power, when their legislature is not in session, to deal with such matters as the lieutenant governor in council deems best. Another province does the same thing, then another and another. Then the Prime Minister comes along and says to this house: Now that the provincial governments have taken these powers, I must be doubly sure of having authority to act with respect to peace, order and good1 government in case- I have to disallow some of this legislation or if there is a dispute, to be able to meet it. It is a sort of competitive arming with respect to legislative and executive power. This is where we find ourselves when we depart from what parliament stands for, namely, a forum where matters can be settled, not as the result of an appeal to power, whether legislative or any other kind, but as the result of an appeal to reason. I think that is as strong an argument as can be put forward against the adoption of these powers which, when parliament is not in session, override the function which parliament itself is expected to perform.

I do not say the provinces were wise in their administrative methods; I do not say they were warranted in making the expenditures they did make or in incurring the liabilities they did incur, but at all events they did what everyone else was doing at that time. This government has done nothing in the way of seeking wider markets except through the agency of the imperial agreements, and even that ray of hope seems to be dimming when we see the reports in the press from day to day as to the attitude of the British government with respect to those agreements so far as they apply to live stock and live stock products. Despite the statement that we hear from time to time that we are to spend a large sum in the construction of public buildings this year I do not believe this will relieve the situation at all. The situation never will be relieved until men get work. To me it seems useless to talk about the extension of credit, the wider circulation of money and all the other panaceas that are offered; if men do not have the privilege of working and earning a livelihood then we will continue to have depression and hard times in this country. No government can assume the responsibility of keeping a large proportion of its people on the payroll of the government; that is out of the question. If fiscal policies are to prevail that will prevent men from getting work and prevent businesses from expanding, the present condition will continue until a change is brought about.

Outside of what appeared in the press, and I did not know it was in the press until the hon. gentleman referred to it, I do not know of any program contemplated by the province.

Is there not an agreement or an understanding between the federal government and the government of Ontario, or the other provincial governments, with respect to the completion of the highway known as the trans-Canada highway? Does this agreement run for only one year or is it continuous? The largest portion of this highway traverses Ontario, and I should like to know if there is not an agreement or understanding that the government will continue to contribute fifty per cent, or forty to sixty, or some such percentage, until it is completed?

The agreements are made from year to year in harmony with the provisions of the various relief acts. The acts expire at the end of each year according to their terms, and any agreements made thereunder expire concurrently. There is no agreement with any province respecting any works because it is obvious that we have no authority to enter into an agreement until this parliament gives us that authority.

That is not what I mean. I realize that the agreement expired on March 31, but this government has made a specific promise that it will contribute fifty per cent of the cost and I should like to know if there is some understanding that that contribution will be continued until the highway is completed. Let me put it in another way. The Prime Minister and his candidates promised that a national highway would be built with funds from the federal exchequer. Apparently they abandoned that idea and offered to make a contribution to the provinces of fifty per cent of the cost. Is there not an agreement that this contribution will be continued until the highway is completed?

I cannot add anything to what I have said already. There is no agreement because there is no authority to make one. Those provinces that find that they cannot get along without assistance from the dominion undoubtedly will approach the dominion with a view to entering into an agreement to take care of the matters to which the hon. member has directed attention, as well as other matters. But at the present time there

is no agreement, there is no understanding, because so far as the government is concerned it would be highly improper to have an understanding or an agreement without any authority for entering into one.

I suppose we shall have to take that just as it is, but once again I submit that it places members in a strange predicament to find themselves voting for a blank cheque to be given to the government when they can get no information as to what is intended. The government made specific promises to the people before they came into power. They cajoled them into voting for this administration, and when my hon. friends got into power they refused to tell the electors what they would do. They will not even give any information to the elected representatives of the people as to what they contemplate. If there is one thing more than another that should open the eyes of members of this house it is the answer which the Prime Minister gave to the hon. member for East Hamilton (Mr. Mitchell). The Prime Minister went to Hamilton and, surrounded by his friends, he got into that sort of humour that I suppose most of us get into at one time or another, though perhaps not with the same spirit as some of us, and he promised the city of Hamilton a building. There are hundreds if not thousands of workmen in Hamilton represented by my good friend from East Hamilton-and he is a very good representative too-and when the hon. gentleman stands on the floor of this house and inquires of the Minister of Labour or of the Prime Minister when it is proposed to start that work what answer does he receive from the right hon. gentleman? He receives one of the most flippant answers ever given in parliament since I have been a member of this house. The hon. gentleman can presuppose this, or he can imagine that, in the hope that some day his expectations may be realized. Is that the sort of answer that should be made by a government who are asking this parliament for a blank cheque?
I cannot see how the government can take this position after four years. There might be an excuse the first year or even the second year; they might say then, "We don't know what will arise; we cannot tell what each province may require." But after four years, surely they ought to be able to inform the members of this house just what the government of Ontario, for instance, or other provinces will wrant. They ought to be able to tell us, after the discussions they have had, whether certain work is to be undertaken in northern Ontario, or in Nova Scotia, or in

Relief Act, 193/f
the province of Quebec, as the case may be, and that as soon as this bill passes they expect to ask for so many millions. They should have some conception of what money is going to be expended and the use to which it will be put. If I were inclined to vote against this measure for any reason whatever, that reason would be the answer which the Prime Minister has just given to the hon. member for East Hamilton. The hon. gentleman has been a very courteous member; he has not been like myself, critical of this government, but has tried to save the government from the mess they got into over the titles question. Well, here is one of the most courteous members of this house rising and asking a question which vitally concerns the workmen of Hamilton: Are they going to be able to save the titles to their little homes? That is the question, and the Prime Minister gives, as I say, the most flippant answer, the sort of answer he would give to a schoolboy.
Yesterday in the course of his remarks the Prime Minister tried to make excuses for the government for the manner in which the federal moneys have been expended, and he compared what the government had done with the Liberal government's attitude towards old age pensions. What a terrible predicament the Prime Minister and the government must find themselves in when they begin to talk about old age pensions and to compare that question with unemployment relief! We made an agreement with the provinces, under authority of an act of parliament, to pay fifty per cent to any province participating in the scheme for the payment of pensions to persons over seventy.
Seventy-five per cent.

I am speaking about the time we were in power. The only difference is that we carried out our promise and you are carrying out yours only twenty-five per cent. The provincial government has full control over the administration of old age pensions-not the municipalities, not unorganized districts, not contractors. The provincial governments are responsible. The Prime Minister yesterday referred to fraudulent cases that had occurred under the old age pensions scheme, and he likened it to the terrible calamity we have now in connection with the expenditures of federal money. Can you imagine the Prime Minister and the government in such straits? Of course, in connection with old age pensions as well as under the Workmen's Compensation Act and the Mothers' Allowance Act, you will find instances here and there where someone 74726-127i
probably gets the benefit of the act when he is not entitled thereto, but I do not suppose that in the whole of Canada there are more than twelve cases; yet the Prime Minister compares that to the expenditure in connection with unemployment relief.
Let me say this, that under the old age pensions legislation the accountant of the Labour department persistently checked up the various provinces, and while it is true that he discovered here and there someone that was not entitled to pension, the province concerned immediately made an adjustment. On the other hand, he found a good many people who were entitled to pension and whom the provinces had denied, and in a great many instances there was an adjustment in this direction. But when hon. gentlemen talk about old age pensions I cannot help observing at this particular time that Ontario through their commissioner is chiselling, whether the Minister of Labour knows it or not, many of the aged people of that province out of their old age pensions. I have several letters, one in particular from a Conservative, a man who was born a Conservative and who I suppose will die one. This man got $20 a month when he reached the age of seventy. That is what the law allows. When his wife attained the age of seventy she also was entitled under the act to $20 per month. And remember, that is the law; it is not what some politician or some commission may say, but it is the law. But the commission in Ontario wrote to this aged couple a letter in which they stated, "Now that you are both receiving the benefit of the old age pension, $30 ought to be sufficient for the two of you." That is chiselling aged people, who are on the brink of the grave, out of $10 a month that is theirs by law. So far as the Prime Minister is concerned, who promised especially in Nova Scotia that one hundred per cent of old age pensions would be paid by the federal government, the less the right hon. gentleman says about old age pensions the better.
I think the Minister of Labour placed on Hansard the record of what the former Liberal government did in 1922 with respect to the administration of unemployment relief. I was not in the House of Commons at that time; I was in the legislature, so I can speak only by the records, but he will find that tiie system that was in vogue in 1922 was instituted by a good Conservative government in October, 1921. That Conservative government initiated the making of agreements not with the provinces but with the municipalities. Now the present Prime Minister says that they were all wrong; that constitutionally
Relief Act, 1934

they had no right to make those agreements with the municipalities, that the action taken was unconstitutional, but nevertheless the government that was defeated in 1921 instituted in October of that year the practice of making agreements with the municipalities. The agreement was extended to some extent since then. At that time it was, I believe, speaking from memory, one-third of the excess cost over normal of works that were done in the winter time. The provision was that this excess cost would be estimated by the dominion government engineers, and this was done. I know from the records, because I had to settle up a good many of those cases even after 1926, that the dominion engineers refused the claims in many instances. For example, some municipalities had put down shovelling snow as excess construction work and there were many other cases of that kind. Those were all checked up by the auditor general and there is no suggestion whatever that through those years there was anything Wrong.
I want again to refer the Minister of Labour to our discussion of yesterday. I know the limitations of the authority of the minister with respect to wages and all that kind of thing, and I am not going to ask him to do anything that I feel I could not do myself were I in that office. But in this particular case provincial governments are, as they have done before, asking the Minister of Labour for contributions to enable them to carry on certain works. While the minister has no jurisdiction in setting wages in the provinces except on dominion works, he has now the jurisdiction to say: "We will give you those contributions on contain conditions," and one of the conditions could be that they pay prevailing rates of wages, or fair wages, or some kind of wages that the minister himself, after consulting with his officers, might determine. He has that power. We do not need to give money away if we do not want to do so, and if we give it away we can give it under any conditions we like to impose.
As I said yesterday, when the bill was first introduced in the house at the special session of 1930, this government gave a specific pledge. I think the hon. member who gave the pledge for the government was the Minister of Justice, who has just left the chamber. We pointed out to him the resolution that was passed in 1900 providing that any contract for works undertaken by anyone with a contribution from this government should include a fair and reasonable rate of wages provision. In 1930 we passed in this chamber

another act providing for eight hours a day and fair rates of wages for government work. The Minister of Public Works, the Minister of Justice and the Prime Minister, if I remember aright, specifically stated, in answer to some of us on this side, that those provinces which were carrying on relief work would have to comply with that resolution and that policy. If that be true, how does it come about that the Ontario government-and I am speaking only about the province in which I reside and about which I know something- with that provision in their agreement and with those regulations to govern them on highway work, dropped the wages of their labourers from thirty-five cents to thirty cents, then from thirty cents down to $5 a month and their board, then raised it to $10 a month and their board, until now, after three years and after some of us have gone through the country shaming that government into action, they have decided all at once to give twenty-five cents an hour? How is it that the Minister of Labour for Canada has not some say in the matter? That is what puzzles me. So far as I can see, the only good to be accomplished by talking on the floor of the House of Commons or outside is to awaken the public to what is going on. I am certain I am not going to get the Minister of Labour, or the hon. member (Mr. Macdougall) who is sitting behind him just now, to agree with me on all points; or.if they do, they will not say so. However, I thank the hon. member for Inverness for agreeing with me for once. I do not speak in the house in the hope of getting the Prime Minister to become a Liberal; I speak in order that the public may understand the treatment that is accorded to the people in northern Ontario and the mishandling and bungling of everything in which the Ontario government has ever taken part. I am appealing to the Minister of Labour to take a hand in this matter and to see that the Ontario government do the right thing. I can recall in 1923 when I was given an acclamation in Ontario-

The hon. member
will never get one again.

I do not want it again;
I want to fight, because the next morning everybody in the street told me he gave me the acclamation. On that occasion there were only two of us who got acclamations. The then member for Kingston, Mr. W. F. Nickle, the only democrat the Conservative party ever had, the man who told the people of Great Britain that we did not want any

Relief Act, 1934
more titles in this country, and I, were the only two who got acclamations. The Conservatives were so pleased with the work I had done in the four previous years that they did' not run a man against me. What happened? The Ferguson government came into power and the highway and road work was shut down overnight, just like the crack of a whip. I knew what was in their minds, but I tried to make excuses for them. I went through my district for six months saying: Be patient; wait till this government find their feet; they will not leave these miles of road leading into the bush, leading to nowhere; give them time. But I found out that it was a designed plot; they were going to tell the people that they had elected a labour man and .to show them that as long as they did not elect a man who would support the Conservative, or the Ferguson, government-because it was never really a Conservative government-they were going to persecute the district. I then went to Hamilton where my hon. friend lives and I made a speech there pointing out that the Ontario government was persecuting a district because I was elected. I went to the head of the lakes and made a similar speech and to Winnipeg and made a similar speech there. And the people, even Conservatives-because there are some good Conservatives; they are pretty hard to find nowadays, but there are some if you look for them-asked the Ontario government: What is all this about? The result was that the Minister of Lands and Forests hied him in a private car to my constituency and put hundreds of men to work-I would not like to say thousands-and then he went to Toronto and said to the newspaper men: "What an awful liar that man Heeoan is; I have more men working in his riding than in any other part of Ontario." So we are speaking here not only because we feel that some time we might touch a sympathetic chord in the heart of the government, but more particularly to let the people of Ontario and of Canada know just what is going on so that they will ask the government whether this is true or not. We ask the Minister of Labour to give us some help, because he is at the head of the department that is supposed to do that. There is only one department of the government of Canada charged with caring for labour, and the officers and the minister of that department ought to have a labour psychology. I agree that there is a limitation to his authority, but we ought at least to have that outlook on life from that department. When we speak about wages we ought to have the sympathetic help of the minister;
he ought to stand in this house and say that if the Ontario government does not increase the wages of these men, we will not give them any further assistance, while if they do increase wages we shall give all the assistance we can consistent with the amount of money we have to spend. In our constituency we had to hold mass meetings of Conservatives, Liberals, Labour, United Farmers of Ontario and everything else in order to get any consideration from the Ontario government for districts for which no Conservative is sitting. I admit that conditions are better now in that regard; they could not allow people to starve to death, because that would attract attention and the rest of Ontario would suffer. But what I am trying to do is to get the assistance of this government and especially of the Minister of Labour. Labour men, Mr. Hutchinson, the member for Kenora in the legislature and a good many others, and I, have been pounding away at the Ontario government for the last three years about the wages they are paying in the camps in northern Ontario, $5 a month in the summer and $10 in the winter. At last after we had called attention for three years to this scandal, the government of Ontario on the eve of an election come out and say they are going to pay twenty-five cents an hour. Of course there will be a lot chiselled off that; they take 50 cents a month for the doctor and so on; they whittle it down so that a man will have about S8 a week. Many of them are married men. Suppose they have a house of which the rent is $15 or $20 a month, and at the end of the month they have $32 to send to their families! I have attended the funerals of some of these men; I have been in their homes when they have been called in from highway work on account of their children being sick through lack of nutrition, or because they were not able to clothe them and send them to school. I have seen some of those men die-they probably would have died anyhow, but I think the Ontario government's scale of pay hastened it somewhat. Now after two or three years, on the eve of an election we have got the Ontario government actually to say to them, not from concern for the working men but in order to try to get a few more votes:	"We have defrauded you
men out of your wages for three years; now we are going to give you back the money that we kept out of your pocket, in the hope that you will vote to put is into power again so that we may sink this province further into debt and increase the taxation of the people." That is the situation in the province of Ontario. I have here for the information of the
Relief Act, 1934

minister a statement made by the Minister of Lands and Forests himself in his own constituency. Speaking in Orillia on February 2, he said:
"I don't consider $10 a month is any wage."
He will not agree that it is even slave wages.
These camps were undertaken to take care of as many idle young men as possible and to give them good board. We give them $10 a month as an allowance and we couldn't give them any more.
In February Mr. Finlayson said: "We cannot give them any more," but now on the eve of an election he says he can give them twenty-five cents an hour. I want to know where the money is coming from. How is it they are in a better position now than when Mr. Finlayson made this statement? I think we are entitled to know this. Mr. Finlayson was one who along with Hon. Charles McCrea and Hon. Howard Ferguson and Hon. George S. Henry and many others took leave from their provincial duties during the last federal election to go up and down the province of Ontario, saying what? Saying that the fact' that there was unemployment in Ontario was due to the fiscal policies of the Liberal government at Ottawa. Now after nearly four years see what Mr. Finlayson says:
Defending the government in regard to present economic conditions the speaker described the depression as an aftermath of war.
Then another minister of the crown in Ontario went to Fort Frances and added insult to injury. Hon. Charles McCrea at Fort Frances last fall said in effect-I have his statement from the local paper, edited by the local Conservative member, so it must be a correct report: "Some will say that the present depression, the troubles we are passing through, were caused by the government at Ottawa or the government in Toronto, but any of you who read or think or exercise ordinary intelligence and sense will know that neither the government at Ottawa nor the provincial government in Toronto is responsible, but that the great war was the cause." That is what gentlemen went about saying. Some of my hon. friends on the other side-I have a lot of good friends there, and hope I shall always keep them-may think that some of us criticize them unduly, but it is because of such trickery as that that we do it. I do not mind losing or winning a football match or a cricket match or an election, but let us do it in a sportsmanlike way; let us not go round blowing about what we are going to do and promising the people what the Prime Minister and members of the pro-

vincial government promised they would do, and then four years afterwards insult the people by saying that if they use common sense or intelligence they will know that we were only trying to deceive or fool them three or four years ago. That is the effect of Mr. McCrea's words.
I want to ask the Minister of Labour now whether he will not insist that some of this money that the government of Ontario has hoarded or has borrowed-I understand they borrowed $40,000,000 recently-will be used to give these men w'ho have been working on the highways their back pay, the money of which they have been robbed. That should be done, instead of increasing their wages now at the eleventh hour, prior to an election. It is their due. These men have been working; they have not been having a good time, as some of the newspapers would have us believe. The foremen have been led to compete against each other to see how many yards of dirt they can move and they, in turn, have had to work their men. They have been firing men because they were not able or willing to work in competition with others. These men have been doing laborious work in the interests of the state, and the state now says, "We do not require these fellows at nil; we are just putting them away up there in the bush."
I understand some question has been raised with regard to the one cent cheque to which I referred yesterday; I understand that the newspaper in Vancouver that published a photograph of this cheque now denies it. I am going to make the statement again, so that it will be understood. The picture of the cheque appears on page 20 of the Vancouver Daily Province of Wednesday, August 16, 1933.
It is cheap trash for a provincial election, and you will not get to first base with it.
I was going to say to the minister, " Render unto Caesar that which is Caesar's; render unto Gott that which is Gott's." That would be about a nickel, or a cent.
You have put that on record about four times.

And you would not understand it if I put it on record again. Eveiy time you squeeze an onion it makes your eyes water. This cheque for one cent was issued by the northern development branch of the province of Ontario and was sent to the editor of the Vancouver Daily Province

Private Bills
by the man who received it. This man's name is C. Oaesar; the cheque was issued on the Canadian Bank of Commerce at Minden, Ontario, and the photograph is headed by the words, "One Month-One Cent." Below the photograph the editor of the newspaper has this to say:
After clothing issued to C. Caesar, worker at camp No. 9, Hall Lake, Minden, Ontario, had been half paid for, he received the cheque shown above for his month's wages. It is a moot question how many dollars will be expended in bookkeeping for the next two or three years carrying this cheque entry forward as an outstanding item, as its owner has requested its return so he may frame it as a souvenir to show to his grandchildren.
I presume he wants to show his grandchildren how the Ontario government paid their workers in 1933. I have other cheques here that have not been cashed.

It costs the country more than one cent to have the hon. member speak. It is a waste of time.
Mr. HEE'NAN:	Pefhaps that is what my
hon. friend thinks, and I cannot blame him if he does think so. Sometimes I wonder if I do much good, but I will say to my hon. friend that he never opens his mouth without giving a grunt like a pig, and that he never rises on the floor of this house except to interfere or heckle. If he were in some parts of the country-

I will stand up now to say
that the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River ought to be ashamed of himself.
I am, because I am talking to you. Every time I talk to my hon. friend I am ashamed of myself.
All this conversation is entirely out of order.
I want to be decent, but I can never be decent when I am speaking to that hon. gentleman.
We know what to expect.

If the chairman cannot
keep that hon. gentleman quiet I will try to do it myself.
You would have a fine time.

All you would have to do would be to give him a little pin prick and he would burst like a bubble. It may be that I am not doing any good, but at least I have awakened some of our editors to the fact that conditions are not what they should be. I have here the Ottawa Citizen of February 10, 1934, from which I am going to read just one sentence. Referring to my remarks in connection with the one cent cheque the Citizen has,this to say:
When Russia has been discussed at Ottawa, there have been contemptuous references to the "slave labour" of that country. At least we ought to set our own house in order before indulging again in such audacious hypocrisy.
This is much more interesting than Ferguson's five cent speeches.

So notwithstanding the
fact that some hon. members may think I am not doing much good, I think perhaps I am doing some good in drawing these matters to the attention of the public. At least I am doing this much good, if my hon. friend can understand it; I have been working on this for over three years, and finally the Ontario government have announced that the wages of the men will be increased to twenty-five cents.

I listen to and understand anything that is sensible.
At six o'clock the Speaker resumed the chair and the house took recess.

speechtext:
On section 2-agreements with provinces.
Mr. HEEN.AN:	While the minister is
waiting for his deputy I want to say a few words by way of concluding my remarks. If the province of Ontario enters into an agreement with the federal government, as undoubtedly the minister expects, I would ask him to see to it that the policy enunciated by this government that fair wages shall be paid on all public works to which contributions are made by this government is carried out. I trust that the minister will insist upon that at this particular time at any rate, even although he has failed to do so in the past.
There is another matter. I recall that wihen the Prime Minister was speaking on the relief bill in 1930 he enunciated a policy of undertaking works for the purpose of supplying work and wages. I think we have got away from the wages end of that policy. It is true that the regulations provided that men in the community in which the work was to be undertaken would be supplied with work, and settlers and others located along the line of the highways would gat the benefit of such work. I would urge upon the minister, and at the same time make an appeal to him, that this government has a duty to perform and that is to see that that policy is carried out. In our district, and I think it applies throughout northern Ontario although I can speak more particularly for the district of Rainy River and Kenora, a great many settlers live during the winter by cutting pulpwood for pulp and paper mills. These mills have been closed down until recently and the settlers have not had the same opportunity to make a living during the winter time. It was expected that the camps would obtain their supplies of vegetables and meats from the settlers along the highway, but the provincial government let a contract to the firm of Crawley and McCracken. We were unable to have these contractors purchase their vegetables and meats from the settlers residing along the highway. The member for Kenora in the legislature went to the government about the matter but they referred him to the contractors. The contractors stated that -they could buy only meats which had gone through a certain inspection. The matter was then referred to me and I took it up with the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir). I must give him credit for doing his share, and I am glad there is one member of the cabinet to whom I can throw a bouquet. I received a telegram from Doctor Grisdale, the deputy minister, under date of December 11, 1931, reading as follows:
Am advised by Mr. Fairbairn, deputy minister agriculture, Toronto, that agreement [Mr. Gott.l
with Crawley and McCracken who have contract to board labour specifies that food shall be good and wholesome. There is no mention of meat inspection. We are ready put man at Dryden or any other place supervise hog slaughterings and issue certificates wholesomeness of product. Please advise with whom we might make contact in order speed up necessary arrangements.
That was in 1931 when there was a plentiful supply of hogs in that particular district. Notwithstanding the fact that this government was making a contribution to the Ontario government, we could not get this contracting firm to purchase, supplies from the farmers in that part of the country. I am safe in saying that hundreds and possibly thousands of bushels of potatoes which these settlers had been encouraged to grow in the belief that they would be purchased as supplies for the camps, rotted in the cellars, while potatoes were purchased in Winnipeg and from eastern points.
There is no doubt that if this matter is brought to the attention of the Ontario government they will claim it has been rectified, but I should like to tell the committee how it has been rectified. The Minister of Lands and Forests made a trip through northern Ontario accompanied by Premier Henry and other members of the cabinet. When this matter was brought to h-is attention by the local member, as well as by settlers in that part of the country, he got up on a public platform and made the announcement that henceforth he would see to it that the contractors purchased potatoes and other vegetables from the settlers in that part of the country. But that promise was never put into practice. The Ontario government is on the eve of an election and the Conservative candidate does not even live in the riding; he lives in the riding of Fort William. This gentleman has placed an advertisement in the papers to the effect that he has made an arrangement with Crawley and McCracken whereby they will purchase their supplies for the camps from the farmers in that vicinity. This is playing politics with unemployment relief, something which the Prime Minister promised would not be done. It is all right for the Minister of Railways (Mr. Manion) to stand up on the floor of this house, as he did the other evening, and say that in connection with all works with which he had anything to do he would give the benefit to his friends and not to his enemies-incidentally, I notice the papers took him to task editorially for making that statement-but I hope the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gordon) will not take a similar position.

Relief Act, 1934
My last appeal to the minister, on this occasion at least, is to ask him to see that these provisions are included in the contract. But a contract is not considered by the Ontario government to be worth very much; they would break a contract to-morrow if they thought it would enhance their political prestige. That is the experience I have had for fifteen or sixteen years. I would much rather say something nice about them, but I cannot find anything nice to say. I appeal to the Minister of Labour to see to it that contractors who are receiving federal money comply with the announced policy of the government.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have
listened carefully to this debate hoping to hear some constructive policy announced by the government to deal with the unemployment problem, but I think it is fair to say that up to the moment the only policy announced is purely negative. It is in direct contradiction of the claims made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) and other members of the government when they went around the country in 1930. The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Heenan) has given examples of the wages paid in the camps up in his part of the country. When the government contribute funds to an enterprise or undertaking, in my judgment they have a direct responsibility to see that a fair rate of wages is paid. I do not think it is fair to the unemployed or to the employed that these men working on a constructive undertaking should be asked to work for $10 a month. In some instances the result has been that a man has received as little as one cent at the end of the month. If these men were placed in the camps simply to be fed, there might be some excuse, but they are taking part in a national enterprise, the construction of a highway from one end of this dominion to the other, and I do not think the government should employ men at a wage scale which no private employer would stoop to pay.
AVe have another example offered us in the
18,000	civil servants receiving less than $1,000 per year who are to have the ten per cent deduction returned to them. It looks to me as though the committee now investigating mass buying should investigate the wages paid by this government as well as those paid by private employers. Perhaps hon. members should not be unmindful of the fact that many within the compass of that 18,000 are postmasters and that this is a strategic move in view of the nearness of an election.
I have listened with keen interest to the remarks of the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River in connection with the policies of the Conservative government of Ontario in this crisis. There is to be an increase in relief. I have no objection to this; I believe it should have been done long ago, but it is passing strange that on the eve of an election a provincial government should find it necessary tc increase relief payments which practically come out of the federal treasury. The workers in these road camps, under this policy, are to have their wages increased to twenty-five cents an hour. It is a pity we cannot have an election every week or so; we should all become rich under those conditions. This afternoon I got a rather stinging reply because I asked when the government expected to be able to put into motion the building policy it had in mind. I hope that is not going to be a purely political policy in view of the forthcoming election. In 1930 it was, "We will cure unemployment or perish in the attempt"; in 1934 the policy is, "Give the electors what they want so that we can get back into power". It is so obvious to even the casual observer that this is the background of the policy.
During the supper hour I was reading a periodical which brings out very clearly the direct responsibility of the government in connection with the payment of wages in any undertaking under their control. The article which I read was an open letter to the Prime Minister in the January number of Chatelaine. It discusses a family, husband and wife and four children. The husband had been out of work for two years but through the assistance given them by their friends they have been able to remain off relief. Eventually this man got a job in one of the camps at a salary of $39.50 a month. The family budget was given as follows: Rent, $12; fuel, $7; light, $1.50; milk, $6; and expenses for the husband's clothes and at the camp, $3.50; drugs, $1, or $31 in all. That left $8.50 to feed and clothe a family of five under their conditions. I will not draw any inferences regarding what has happened in other countries; they have to work out their own destiny their own way. We however have a direct responsibility in relation to a vital question such as this.
Under the widow's pension legislation of the province this family would have been entitled, if the husband were dead, to allowances equivalent to $58.50 per month, so that the family would have been better off had the husband and father passed to the great beyond than they are while he is trying to make
Relief Act, 1934

a contribution to the building-up of the country. Had he been an invalid-he would have been treated as a child-he would have received S67.05 per month. In my judgment this shows very clearly the responsibility of any governmental agency in the employment of men who after all are their fellow Canadians.
I should like to have seen the government bring down something very definite instead of giving us a reiteration of the policy of the dole -because we might as well be frank about it- which has been in existence during the last three or four years. I should like to have seen them move in the direction of getting rid of some of the slum districts in the larger centres. I should like to have seen them expand a building program to provide houses for the people of the country. One could quote figures showing the real shortage that exists at the moment. In my city rents are increasing because of the contraction of available houses owing to the depression. I think the government has a direct responsibility in that regard, just as much of a responsibility to the average man and woman in the street as it shows in its policy in connection with one or two big undertakings which have been assisted. I do not say this critically but by way of comparison; for if it is sound and logical to come to the assistance of one form of organization which the government feels necessary to the life of the dominion, I think it is just as essential that the government should [DOT]come to the assistance of those who find themselves in a position such as I have indicated, over which they have no control.
I must therefore express my disappointment in the attitude of the government with regard to unemployment. I cannot say that I wholly agree with the leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) in the view he takes of the blank cheque aspect of the legislation. I would give the government any kind of cheque if only they would implement the promises they made in the last election. I think the Canadian people are all of one mind on that point. I am mindful of the fears of the leader of the opposition, but I would point this out. Liberty is not merely a right; it has been obtained by fighting and sacrifice. It is an asset that has been dearly won by the Anglo-Saxon people and it can be maintained in a democracy only if the citizens are willing to grant the state the powers they think necessary in an emergency of this description. I believe you have to choose between that and a dictatorship. I do not believe anything can be done under a dictatorship that cannot be done in a [Mr. Mitchell 1
democracy, and I am of the opinion that when the history of this period is written it will be found that those countries who observed most closely the spirit of democratic institutions will be those that will have passed through this trial and will most successfully cope with the inevitable problems that will confront them then. I believe that sincerely. At the same time, I do not think that we should deny those who have the responsibility of leadership and government the freedom to lead, though I think that responsibility should be definite and for a fixed period. I think this also, that you must retain control over those charged with responsibility; you must leave yourself the right, I might almost say the divine right, to change them. I have never held the opinion that we should permit legislative medicine to be prescribed for us. I think it can be safely said that this House of Commons is a pretty fair cross-section of the Canadian people. What I like about democracy is that it is so human; it is a system of government in which you suffer for your own sins. If you elect t'he wrong kind ,of people, you suffer accordingly.

speechtext: My hon. friend asks what wages were paid on that work. Wages as such have never been considered as being paid. These men were placed there on a sustenance basis. They were given their food and their shelter, and their clothing and equipment to fit them for their work. In addition, they were given an allowance of twenty cents a day, which was given not as wages but to enable them to provide themselves with certain necessaries such as shaving equipment, toilet articles, tooth brushes, soap, towels and so forth, and tobacco. The twenty cents a day was not paid to these men as a wage. They were there simply on a sustenance basis. I wish to discuss the

Last week Mr. Finlay-son stated that work on the trans-Canada highway would be started west of the town of Hearst. This is a message that has been received with great joy in my section of the country and also in the riding represented by the Minister of Labour, and I should like to receive from the minister an assurance that the government of Ontario has approached him in this matter in his capacity as head of the unemployment relief administration.
There is one question which is of very great importance to our section and it is this. Construction of the highway west of Hearst is a problem that must have been studied carefully during the last three years-that is, the routing of the road. If the road swings back immediately south of Hearst it will have no significance to our section from the point of view of tourist traffic. The routing of the road west of Hearst should go westerly following the National Transcontinental highway for a considerable distance, at least as far west as Nakina. I draw this to the attention of the minister because I think he is familiar with the situation so far as the trans-Canada highway is concerned, and I think that sufficient time has been given the provincial government to study the proper routing of the road.
I should be glad if the minister could tell the committee that what Mr. Finlayson has

said will be carried out in the course of the summer, and that the work will be started very soon in the spring.
There is another matter which is discussed a good deal in our section of the country, and that is the land-bonusing scheme. I believe the impression has been created in northern Ontario that the scheme will be financed partly by the federal government and partly by the treasury of Ontario, and this is one of the best ways whereby to remedy the dire situation that exists among our settlers in northern Ontario. It may be suggested that such promises are made only in anticipation of an election, but I do not take it in that sense. I am sure that if this promise were implemented it would provide an excellent way of improving the condition of our settlers, and the beneficial results would be reflected not only throughout Ontario but in the whole of Canada.
Another matter in which I know the department is interested is the back to the land movement. I would point out to the minister that this year most of the people settled under the scheme in northern Ontario will find it absolutely impossible out of the $10 a month that they receive, or, to be precise, out of the $200 they get yearly for three years, to supply themselves with the necessary seed grain. This being so, I think that everyone will realize at once that unless the necessary seed is given them free the people who have settled under the back to the land movement will find it utterly impossible to get along this season, because they cannot provide seed for themselves this year. It is true that some of these people have been operating under the scheme for the last two years, and some settled last year. The question may be asked: How is it that these new settlers did not find it possible to grow sufficient grain to supply their own requirements for the coming season? Well, the answer will suggest itself to anyone who is at all familiar with the climatic conditions that prevailed last summer in that part of the country. The conditions were such last year on account of the drought that practically no grain could be grown on the land by these people, and that should convince the committee and the minister that it would be impossible for these people, out of the $200 they receive under the tripartite arrangement, the contributors being the municipal, provincial and federal authorities, to provide sufficient funds to buy the necessary seed grain. I believe that the government of Ontario led the settlers in my own section of northern Ontario as a whole to understand that they would be

supplied with seed this spring. Now, I do not believe in giving a wrong impression of any situation, but I am bound to say to the minister that in my section not five per cent of the settlers will be in a position this spring to buy seed grain, and I know that if the grain is not given them free most of the area ploughed last fall will remain uncultivated. It will be absolutely impossible for these people to put the ground under crop, and from that statement the committee will realize that the situation will be aggravated next fall; it will be worse than it is this spring. I do not know how far the federal authority will go in supplying the seed grain to the settlers who have been on these farms a number of years, but I do know that under the back to the land scheme the government will have to find funds sufficient to supply with seed for the coming spring the new men placed under the direct policy of the federal government.

Marie, that would not provide a solution of the problem from our point of view, because it would not give the communication to which we are entitled. I should like the minister therefore to be kind enough to answer the three questions I have submitted to him.
